title: AI earnings shield US stocks, but bond risks rise: Jefferies' Wood
source_used: The Economic Times (full text from the page's article body markup)
key_facts: Jefferies global equity strategist Chris Wood says in his newsletter Greed & Fear that US stocks have largely shrugged off rising bond yields and geopolitical tension this year, helped by strong earnings growth from the AI capital spending cycle.
Still, he says the bond market is reaching levels where risks to equities are growing, particularly with the US Federal Reserve turning more hawkish (more inclined to keep or raise interest rates).
US 10-year and 30-year government bond yields hit 5.34% and 5.69%, their highest since April 2002 and May 2002.
US stocks usually do badly before midterm elections and rally after, but that has not happened this year, mainly because of AI-driven earnings growth, Wood says.

Wood names three issues for investors: how long the AI capex cycle lasts and whether the huge spending earns adequate returns; a renewed realisation that G7 government bonds are in a structural bear market; and shifting geopolitics.
The Economic Times links the yield rise to last week's slide in Indian stocks, which posted an eighth straight weekly loss.
quote_evidence: Still, the bond market is now reaching levels where the risks to equities are growing, most particularly with the US Federal Reserve turning more hawkish, he said in his newsletter Greed & Fear.

The yield on the US ten-year and 30-year government bonds hit 5.34% and 5.69% respectively to their highest levels since April 2002 and May 2002, partly contributing to last week's slide in Indian equities, which posted their eighth straight week of losses till Friday.

According to Wood, investors are facing three issues: the first, and perhaps most important for equities, is the duration of the AI capex cycle and whether there will be adequate returns from the massive spending.
why_it_matters_hint: A well-known strategist says AI-driven profits are holding up US stocks while bond yields at 2002 highs are becoming the bigger risk.
event_date: 2 Oct 2026 (Seeking Alpha reported Wood's note that day; the Economic Times piece is dated 3 Oct 2026)
